acceptedAnswer.text: The equation is no longer quadratic: it becomes bx + c = 0, a linear equation with the single solution x = −c ÷ b (if b ≠ 0). The quadratic formula divides by 2a, so it cannot be used. This calculator tells you the linear solution instead.

mainEntity.name: How do complex roots appear on a graph?

acceptedAnswer.text: When Δ < 0 the parabola does not touch the x-axis, so there are no real roots. The complex roots p ± qi have the real part p = −b ÷ 2a, which is the axis of symmetry, and the imaginary part q = √(−Δ) ÷ 2a, which measures how far the vertex is from the axis.

mainEntity.name: Why is the vertex’s x-coordinate the midpoint of the roots?

acceptedAnswer.text: The two roots are −b ÷ 2a ± √Δ ÷ 2a, so their average is −b ÷ 2a — exactly the vertex’s x-coordinate. A parabola is symmetric about its axis.

mainEntity.name: What is the sum and product of the roots?

acceptedAnswer.text: By Vieta’s formulas, x₁ + x₂ = −b ÷ a and x₁ · x₂ = c ÷ a. They let you check your answers: for x² − 5x + 6 the roots 2 and 3 add to 5 and multiply to 6.

mainEntity.name: When should I use factoring or completing the square instead?

acceptedAnswer.text: Factoring is quickest when the roots are integers or simple fractions. Completing the square derives the formula and gives the vertex form. The quadratic formula always works, whatever the coefficients.

mainEntity.name: Can the coefficients be decimals or fractions?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Enter decimals directly. Exact radical forms are shown when the coefficients are integers; otherwise you get precise decimal roots.
